cards.explanation: The answer is in the days of David. The verse says 22,600 of Tola's descendants were numbered in their genealogies as mighty men of valor in the days of David, Israel's king. That's a whole stadium of strong folks from one family, friends. I'd hate to be the guy picking teams against them.

The answer is False. The text gives the reason in plain words: "…for they had many wives and children." Hired soldiers from other lands aren't the reason it names, friends. The 36,000 troops are tied to that big household. That's a family reunion with a draft number.

The answer is True. The text says, "Their father Ephraim mourned for many days, and his relatives came to comfort him." Ezer and Elead were killed, and their father grieved them. I like that his relatives came to him, friends. I think that's what comfort looks like.

The answer is tragedy. The verse says Ephraim named him Beriah "…because tragedy had come upon his house." The name carries the memory of what his family went through. I think it shows that he didn't pretend the hurt wasn't there. The Bible keeps it real, friends.

The answer is True! Sheerah built Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah too. That's three towns, friends. In a list where most lines are just names, she gets a building permit. I've stamped a lot of cookies and never built a single town, so I'm impressed.

The answer is Joshua. The list ends with "Nun his son, and Joshua his son." This is the same Joshua who took over leading Israel after Moses died (Joshua 1:1-2). A long line of fathers and sons, friends, and it lands on a name that matters. I'd have cheered if I could.

The answer is Aijalon for the first blank and Gath for the second. Beriah and Shema were heads of families living in Aijalon, and the same verse says they drove out the inhabitants of Gath. Two things in one sentence, friends. That's a busy verse. Earlier in the passage, the natives of Gath are the ones who killed Ephraim's sons (1 Chronicles 7:21). I'll just let everybody notice that themselves.

The answer is Jerusalem. The verse says all these heads of families, the chiefs according to their genealogies, lived in Jerusalem. After all those towns and moves, friends, a whole group lands in one city. A long list finally gets an address.

The answer is Saul. The text says, "Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul…" This is the same Saul who became Israel's king (1 Samuel 11:15). After all those names, friends, a familiar one finally walks in.

The answer is True. The verse says Saul was the father of "…Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal." Jonathan is the first one named, friends. Four sons in a row, and one name you probably know.

The answer is archers. The verse says Ulam's sons were "…mighty men of valor, archers…" It also says they had 150 sons and grandsons in all. That's a lot of family in one verse, friends. I'd stay out of Ulam's backyard.
